title: Did Coca-Cola Really Make Santa Red?
subtitle: A bishop, a New York dream, one reindeer then eight, Nast's wartime Santa, and the color of his coat before 1931

segments.text: Every December, the same story comes back. Santa Claus wears red because of Coca-Cola. In the nineteen thirties, the company's advertisements showed a warm, round Santa in a red suit, and many people believe that is where the red suit began. It is a good story. But the older pictures are still here: prints, books, poems and magazine covers. We can put them in order. So, did Coca-Cola really make Santa red?

In this episode, we follow Santa through time: a bishop in the fourth century, a dream in a New York history book, a little book with a single reindeer, a poem with eight, a drawing made in wartime, and the color of his coat, long before nineteen thirty-one.

The story begins with a real name. Nicholas was a bishop of Myra, a town in what is now southern Turkey, in the fourth century. Beyond that, almost nothing about his life is historically certain. The stories of his kindness came later, and they made him a saint of gift-giving.

In ten eighty-seven, sailors from Bari, in southern Italy, took his remains from Myra and carried them home to their own city. In parts of Europe, children came to receive gifts on his feast day, December the sixth, and on the evening before. In the Netherlands, he became Sinterklaas, and he is still dressed as a bishop.

Across the ocean, New York writers took up the name. In eighteen twelve, in the expanded second edition of his comic History of New York, Washington Irving described a dream. In it, the good Saint Nicholas came riding over the tops of the trees, in the same wagon in which he brings his yearly presents to children. There is no sleigh here yet, and no reindeer.

Nine years later, in eighteen twenty-one, a small illustrated book printed in New York, The Children's Friend, changed that. Its first page begins: Old Santeclaus with much delight, his reindeer drives this frosty night. The picture shows his sleigh, pulled by a single reindeer. And in one surviving copy, now at Yale University, Santeclaus is already wearing a red coat.

Two years later, in eighteen twenty-three, a newspaper in Troy, New York, printed an unsigned poem, Account of a Visit from St. Nicholas. The editor wrote that he did not know who had sent it. It was later published under Clement Clarke Moore's name, and in eighteen forty-four it appeared in his own book of poems. Its Saint Nicholas is chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf. He is dressed all in fur, from his head to his foot. He drives a miniature sleigh with eight tiny reindeer. His cheeks are like roses, his nose like a cherry. But the poem never gives his clothes a color.

Magazines carried Santa to many more readers. In eighteen fifty-eight, Harper's Weekly printed Santa Claus and His Presents, drawn by a young Winslow Homer. Soon after, Thomas Nast began drawing Santa for the same magazine, and he kept drawing him for more than twenty years. In January eighteen sixty-three, during the American Civil War, his Santa visited a Union army camp, in a coat of stars and striped trousers. In eighteen eighty-one came his Merry Old Santa Claus: round, bearded, with a pipe and an armful of toys. These pictures were printed in black and white.

Color prints tell us more. In a book of the poem published in Boston in eighteen sixty-four, Santa's suit is a pale, earthy brown. So his coat was not fixed. But red kept coming back. In December nineteen oh two, and again in nineteen oh four, the magazine Puck put a red-suited Santa on its Christmas covers, decades before the famous soft-drink paintings.

The illustrator Haddon Sundblom began painting Santa for Coca-Cola in nineteen thirty-one, and he painted his last one for the company in nineteen sixty-four. The company's own history says it plainly. Santa appeared in a red coat before Sundblom painted him.

So Coca-Cola did not invent the red suit. But year after year, its advertisements showed the same warm, very human Santa, and helped make him familiar to a very wide audience. The color was older. What the advertisements helped spread was one friendly face.

So, did Coca-Cola really make Santa red? No. A red coat appears more than a century earlier. What changed over time was almost everything else. A bishop became a visitor in the night. The visitor rode a wagon, then a sleigh with one reindeer, then eight. A poem dressed him in fur. And printers spread many versions of him, until one became the face most of us know.
Every story has an origin. Sometimes, it begins with a bishop, and printers finish it.
